 The Polls Have Closed. What Happens Now?
 Here are six things to know about what happens after the polls close.
 By Camilla Rodriguez Guzman 
  |  
 October 22, 2026 
 State Legislatures News Elections 
 (Jillian Cain/Getty Images) 
 For most voters, Election Day ends when they cast their ballot and begin watching the returns. But while the polls may have closed, the election process is far from over. Election officials continue counting ballots, verifying results, conducting audits and completing other important steps before the results become official.
 Here are six things to know about what happens after the polls close.
 1. Election night results and ‘called’ races are unofficial
 On election night, the results seen on government websites or on television, news websites or social media are unofficial. News organizations make projections and may even “call” races as soon as election offices begin reporting unofficial results. But those results are not final and are subject to change as additional votes are counted. This is normal and happens in every election. Official election results come much later once states have completed counting every single ballot.
 2. The vote counting continues after Election Day
 The most common deadline for absentee/mail ballots is when the polls close on Election Day. Thirty-five states require absentee/mail ballots to be received on or before Election Day. Fifteen states, along with Washington, D.C., Guam, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, accept and count absentee/mail ballots received after Election Day, if they are postmarked on or before Election Day. In other states, these provisions may also apply to military and overseas voters.
 The 15 states that accept postmarked ballots also establish deadlines for when ballots must be received by election officials. For example, Oregon requires ballots to be received at the office of the county clerk within seven days after the election. Texas requires ballots to be received by 5 p.m. on the day after the election.
 3. Election officials finalize the results
 A canvass is the post-election counting of all valid ballots cast in the election; it ultimately leads to the certification of final election results. During canvassing, states verify voters’ signatures, review provisional ballots and determine voter eligibility to ensure that all eligible ballots are counted. Because this process takes time, most states set deadlines for local and state election officials to complete the canvass.
 Local canvass deadlines range from the day after the election in Alaska to 30 days afterward in many California elections.
 State canvass dates vary significantly. In Oklahoma, the canvass takes place on the Friday after the election, as long as no contest has been filed. In Missouri, it takes place on the second Tuesday in December for most elections.
 4. Only certified results are the official election results
 Certifying the results of an election includes a formal process where election officials attest that the election results are true and accurate. For some states, certifying the election results comes after the canvass process or after the post-election audit; in other states, the audit may be performed after results are certified.
 The process for certifying election results varies across state and local jurisdictions, according to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission. State and federal results are canvassed and certified locally, then aggregated and certified at the state level. Certification may be conducted by the secretary of state, governor, an appointed elections director, a multimember board or another state-level entity. At the local level, certification often is handled by a multimember board or an elected official, such as a county auditor or municipal clerk.
 Local and state certification deadlines vary. For example, in Arkansas, local election results for offices other than president must be certified within 15 days after the election. Results for congressional races must be certified by the secretary of state within 30 days after receiving the county election returns.
 5. Post-election audits check for accuracy
 Post-election audits help confirm that votes were counted accurately by reviewing the equipment and procedures used during the election. All 50 states and Washington, D.C., conduct some type of post-election audit, but the requirements and procedures vary by state. State legislatures decide what type of audit process to require.
 The traditional post-election audit is the most common type of audit and is currently used in 36 states. Traditional post-election tabulation audits are typically conducted manually and compare voting machine tabulations with the paper record. Some states have a process by which some parts or all of the audit can be conducted electronically.
 Other common audit types are risk-limiting audits and procedural audits .
 Depending on state law, post-election audits may be conducted by local election officials, state election officials or other designated authorities. For example, Alabama requires a probate judge to conduct the audit, while states such as Idaho, Louisiana, Mississippi, Nebraska and Vermont assign that responsibility to the secretary of state. In California and Colorado, post-election audits are conducted by local election officials under the oversight of the secretary of state. Poll watchers and appointed representatives of political parties may be allowed to observe the process.
 Although post-election audits can lead to a full recount if errors are detected, they differ from a recount in that they are conducted regardless of the margins of victory. Recounts are most often triggered or requested if there is a tight margin of victory.
 The completion deadlines for post-election audits vary. Thirty-one states and Washington, D.C., require post-election audits to be finalized before an election can be certified. Ten states complete the post-election audit after certification of the election results. The remaining nine states do not specify a completion deadline.
 6. Winning the election doesn’t mean taking office immediately
 In November, voters in 46 states will head to the polls to elect 6,139 state legislators.
 Newly elected candidates do not take office immediately after the election. Instead, they begin their terms on a date specified by law. Elected members of the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate take office on Jan. 3, 2027.
 Start dates for state and local offices vary by jurisdiction. In California, for example, legislators will begin work on Dec. 7, while state officers including the governor take office on Jan. 4, 2027. In Indiana, certain state and county officials will begin their terms on Jan. 1, 2027, and in Alabama, nonfederal offices will be inaugurated on Jan. 18, 2027.
 For more information, visit NCSL’s series on post-election processes. 
 Camilla Rodriguez Guzman is a policy analyst in NCSL’s Elections and Redistricting Program.
